Opponents of the proposed tax have raised hundreds of millions of dollars to defeat it, and most of that funding has come from the billionaires themselves. Recent polls show that the so-called billionaire tax is losing steam among California voters.
Arguably the two most reputable pollsters of California are UC Berkeley's Institute of Governmental Studies and the Public Policy Institute of California.
Both found last month that support for Proposition 40, which would impose a one-time, 5% wealth tax on California residents worth more than $1 billion, has declined, leaving neither side with a clear lead.
The results are a departure from earlier surveys by the same pollsters, which both found the "Yes" side leading the "No" in their September polls.
The October poll from the Public Policy Institute of California, a nonpartisan think tank, found that 46% of likely voters said they would vote yes on the proposed tax, down from 52% in September: The numbers in opposition moved in mirror image, with the share opposing the measure growing from 46% to 52%.
Polling from Berkeley IGS found a similar trend.
In October, IGS found 50% of likely voters intended to vote no on the tax, while 42% planned to vote yes, with 8% undecided.
A month earlier, just 42% planned to vote no on the tax, while 45% planned to vote yes.
Not every poll found that support for the tax is lagging.
In early October, a Politico poll found that 46% of likely voters planned to vote Yes on Prop.

In summary
Californians are voting on 14 ballot measures, including propositions on taxes, voting, healthcare, housing and the environment. It’s a lot to take in, but we’re here to help.
Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called.
Yes, the much talked-about billionaire tax (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-billionaire-tax-explainer/) is on the ballot this November, but it’s just one of 14 statewide propositions.
If you’re not a policy wonk who knows the ins and outs of state election, tax or environmental law, don’t worry — you’re not alone, and we’re here to help. The CalMatters voter guide (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/?ref=homepage&module=spotlight) has full explainers, videos and even quizzes (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/propositions/quizzes/) to help you decide how these measures line up with your values and priorities.
But if you do want the tl;dr on who is supporting what, here’s an even shorter, last-minute summary.
Taxes: Props. 2, 3, 40, 41, 42 and 43
If it seems like this year’s ballot has an unusually high number of tax-related ballot propositions (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/tax-propositions-ballot-measures/), well, you’re right. It does.
Prop. 2 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-2-rainy-day-fund/) would allow the state to deposit more money into its reserves (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-proposition-2-explained/), otherwise known as the rainy day fund. The state has strict rules about how much money it can save for lean times in part because of limits imposed during the state’s 1970s taxpayer revolt. But California also has a fairly volatile tax system that rises and falls with the incomes of its highest earners. Democrats want more flexibility to sock money away for downturns. Many Republicans say leftover money should go to taxpayers, rather than sit in state coffers.
Prop. 3 (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-3-california/) would turn a temporary income tax for high earners (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-3-california/) into a permanent law. The tax, which hits those with individual income over $360,000, was enacted as a quick fix in 2012, with most of the money going to support K-12 education and community colleges. Now the state’s largest teachers union wants to make the tax permanent (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/proposition-3-california-schools-funding/), but opponents say California already has some of the highest taxes in the country (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/proposition-3-temporary-tax-permanent/).
Prop. 40, otherwise known as the billionaire tax, (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-billionaire-tax-explainer/) is hands-down the highest profile and the most expensive proposition campaign this year. It would enact a one-time 5% tax on billionaires’ net worth, raising roughly $100 billion over five years, according to the healthcare workers union that put the measure on the ballot. Proponents argue that these ultra-wealthy Californians are already getting federal tax cuts and that the money will help healthcare programs (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/07/proposition-40-billionaire-tax-health/) that face state and federal funding cuts (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uY2CKS4w58M). But business leaders point out that California relies on these billionaires for tax revenue (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/06/california-unions-billionaire-tax-ballot/), and if they leave, the state could suffer. (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/07/billionaire-tax-risks-proposition-40/) Even some healthcare organizations, such as Planned Parenthood, oppose Prop. 40, because they are concerned the money won’t actually help stave off state and federal funding cuts. (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-billionaire-tax-explainer/)
Prop. 40 is so controversial that its opponents have two rival ballot measures, Prop. 41 and Prop. 42 (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/09/california-wealth-tax-prop-40-41-42/), which, if approved, would thwart the billionaire tax. A yes vote for either of these two ballot measures would invalidate the billionaire tax.
Prop. 43 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-43-tax-threshold/) would make it harder for local citizen-driven tax referenda to pass. Currently, these local tax measures only need a majority to win. If Prop. 43 passes, they would need two-thirds of the vote. Proponents say Prop. 43 closes a loophole (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/california-constitution-proposition-43-taxes/) in election tax law. Opponents say it’s anti-democratic. (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/proposition-43-taxes-minority-rule/)
Should California borrow money for housing and medical research?
The state can quickly raise lots of cash by selling bonds (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/bond-measures-on-california-ballot/) to investors, but selling too many bonds risks saddling the state with debt.
Prop. 1 (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/10/prop-1-housing-bond/) would authorize the state to borrow up to $11.25 billion toward housing construction and renovations, mostly for rental units. Many developers and local governments that receive the money would have to reserve a portion of it for affordable housing for low-income renters or for specialized housing that serves the homeless. Some money would also be earmarked to support first-time homebuyers, veterans, farmworkers, students and California’s tribal communities.
Prop. 37 (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/prop-37-explained-homeownership/) would create a loan fund that helps middle-class homebuyers with their down payment. It’s technically a $25 billion bond, though the money would get paid back slowly by homebuyers rather than from taxpayers. If passed, most California renters would qualify. Proponents, including unions, real estate developers and the Democratic Party, say the proposition could make homebuying accessible, but opponents say it has a number of problems that could prevent the program from actually happening, or worse, that it could put homebuyers in greater debt.

Prop. 38 (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/) would pump $8.4 billion in state funding to immunology research — but with a catch. About half the money would go to one nonprofit organization (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-38-california/), most likely the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy. Gary K. Michelson, the institute’s co-founder, put this proposition on the ballot.
Changing election laws
These ballot propositions could shape how the candidates raise money and how recall elections operate. Voters will also weigh in on a voter ID proposal.
Prop. 4 (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-proposition-4-explainer/) would allow the state and local governments to create public financing for political campaigns. Proponents, including the California Democratic Party, argue it could help cap political spending because candidates usually have to accept certain spending limits in exchange for access to public money. Opponents say the proposal could force taxpayers to chip in money for candidates they don’t support. Research on the effectiveness of public financing for political campaigns is mixed.
Prop. 5 (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-election-proposition-5-explainer/) would modify the rules surrounding California’s recall elections. Currently, a recall election asks voters whether they want to oust the officeholder and who they want instead. A yes vote on Prop. 5 would make it so that recall elections only ask whether voters want to remove the elected official from office. If recalled, another election would determine who should replace the officeholder. The Democratic Party supports this proposition. Republicans oppose it.
Prop. 39 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-39-voter-id/) would increase identification requirements for California voters. To register, voters are already required to declare in writing that they are U.S citizens. This proposition would require voters to show proof of citizenship before casting their vote. Republicans argue the proposition would put California in line with many other states (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/voter-identification-proposition-39-elections/) and that it will crack down on voter fraud, which is rare. (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/05/gop-continues-voter-fraud-narrative/) They’ve spent over $36 million supporting the proposition, almost half of it from Illinois billionaire Richard Uihlein (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-election-voter-id-proposition-39/). Democrats say Prop. 39 could create “unnecessary barriers,” (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/voter-id-barriers-proposition-39/) especially for immigrants and low-income Californians who lack a driver’s license.
Other stuff: Healthcare and the environment
Anyone can place a proposition on California ballots if they follow the right procedures and get enough signatures, but special interest groups, such as unions and pro-business organizations, do it more often than most.
Prop. 44 (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/10/union-billionaire-prop-44-clinic/) comes from the same healthcare workers union that put the billionaire tax on the ballot. It would force health clinics to spend at least 90% of their annual revenue on patient care. The union, Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, argues Prop. 44 is needed to keep CEO salaries in check and ensure clinics are spending money on patients. The Democratic Party and healthcare associations oppose it, saying it will create unnecessary regulation at a time when clinics are already facing financial pressures from federal budget cuts.
Prop. 45 (https://calmatters.org/environment/2026/10/prop-45-california-ceqa-explained/), sponsored by the pro-business California Chamber of Commerce, could pare down California’s landmark environmental review law, known as CEQA. The 1970 law requires agencies to consider environmental harm before building, but developers say the law is often a tool to delay much-needed affordable housing (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/07/proposition-45-housing-environmental-reform/) and infrastructure projects. Environmentalists say approving Prop. 45 could be “disastrous” (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/07/proposition-45-environment-health-protections/) for communities that live near industrial pollution.
If you want more information, remember that all of this information, and much more, is available in the CalMatters voter guide (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/?ref=homepage&module=spotlight).

**Getting your Trinity Audio player ready...**
Support for a proposed one-time 5% tax on billionaires’ wealth is waning among California voters, according to a new independent poll released this week.
Proposition 40, a highly contentious November ballot measure, has the support of 46% of likely voters in the latest survey from the Public Policy Institute of California — down from last month’s poll, which showed it had majority support with 52% of likely voters in favor.
In the latest poll, which was conducted between Oct. 16 and 22 by the San Francisco-based nonpartisan research group, 52% of likely voters were opposed and 2% were undecided.
The initiative also saw a 9-percentage-point decline in support among likely Bay Area voters, from 58% in support last month to 49% in support in the latest survey.
The PPIC surveyed 1,086 likely voters and the poll had a margin of error of 3.8 percentage points.

Arguably the two most reputable pollsters of California are UC Berkeley's Institute of Governmental Studies and the Public Policy Institute of California.
Both found last month that support for Proposition 40, which would impose a one-time, 5% wealth tax on California residents worth more than $1 billion, has declined, leaving neither side with a clear lead.
The results are a departure from earlier surveys by the same pollsters, which both found the "Yes" side leading the "No" in their September polls.
The October poll from the Public Policy Institute of California, a nonpartisan think tank, found that 46% of likely voters said they would vote yes on the proposed tax, down from 52% in September: The numbers in opposition moved in mirror image, with the share opposing the measure growing from 46% to 52%.
Polling from Berkeley IGS found a similar trend.
In October, IGS found 50% of likely voters intended to vote no on the tax, while 42% planned to vote yes, with 8% undecided.
A month earlier, just 42% planned to vote no on the tax, while 45% planned to vote yes.

# Latest Polls In 2026 Midterms: Democrat Adam Hamilton Ahead In Kansas Senate Race In 2 Polls
## What do polls on California's billionaire tax indicate?
Proposition 40, which would impose a one-time tax on the roughly 260 California billionaires equal to 5% of their wealth, appears to be a toss-up, though significant shares of voters are undecided.
A Politico survey released Oct. 19 by the nonpartisan University of California Berkeley Jack Citrin Center for Public Opinion Research found 46% support Proposition 40 and 43% are against it.
An NBC/Telemundo poll taken by the nonpartisan firm Mason-Dixon Polling & Research and released Sept. 30 found 48% of respondents support the tax, 38% oppose it and 14% are undecided.
The University of California Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies, also considered nonpartisan, found 45% support Proposition 40 and 42% oppose it in a survey released Sept.
25. Conservative-leaning organizations found more opposition.
A poll released Friday from GOP-aligned pollster McLaughlin & Associates for the California Post found 53% oppose the tax, compared to 35% who support it, while 12% are undecided.
A survey released Oct. 9 from the conservative think tank, the Manhattan Institute, found 50% of voters oppose the measure, 35% support it and 15% are undecided.

DRIVING THE DAY — Gavin Newsom redoubled his support for Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed , after his rival in the primary, Haley Stevens , made a shock endorsement of Republican Mike Rogers on Sunday morning.
But Newsom’s response — a post on X (https://x.com/GavinNewsom/status/2116963882321547624?a=a81hx_WxO-5-yTzeKvQ&s=20) affirming his support for El-Sayed without mentioning Stevens — was notably less lacerating than other Democrats, including Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer , who said Stevens committed a “despicable betrayal.”
Appearing on the YouTube show 2Way (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ppJFvSvw5yY), Newsom was asked by conservative co-host Larry O’Connor whether Democrats were being hypocritical after years of urging Republicans to choose country over party and break with Trump.
“I don’t know enough about what ultimately led her to make that decision outside of what she said in that video. And she certainly has the right to do that, and I don’t condemn her on that basis. I don’t agree with her, and made that point clear,” Newsom said.
That was not sufficient for frequent Newsom antagonist Rep. Ro Khanna , who posted on X (https://x.com/RoKhanna/status/2117066889553650073?a=eHCTLwwsrEUVOUhEhso&s=20) linking the lack of condemnation to Newsom’s opposition to the billionaires tax, adding Newsom’s “Big Tent is just standing for nothing.”
Meanwhile, Kamala Harris recorded robo-calls supporting El-Sayed in Michigan. She did not make a public comment about Stevens’ endorsement of Rogers.
BEYOND THE TOPLINE — The California governor’s race sits at the top of the ticket, but Xavier Becerra vs. Steve Hilton isn’t where the drama is. That’s down the ballot.
These are the races that POLITICO California reporters will be refreshing on election night. Among them are a ballot measure that tests just how much voters want to stick it to billionaires, the Democratic incumbents who may be swept out by demands for generational change, and a pair of contests in Los Angeles that could establish democratic socialist dominance in the nation’s second largest city.
Here are our picks of the top races to watch.
Melanie Mason: Yes, the Los Angeles mayor’s race is the marquee contest in the city (more on that below). But don’t sleep on the little-watched city attorney’s race, where Marissa Roy , a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, appears poised to defeat (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-28/marissa-roys-lead-grows-over-john-mckinney-in-la-city-attorney-race) John McKinney , a centrist Democrat running on a law-and-order platform. While Nithya Raman ’s relationship with DSA has been fraught, Roy’s race has been a top priority for the group. If both Raman and Roy win their races, it would mean candidates from the insurgent left will occupy all three citywide offices (controller Kenneth Mejia , also a progressive, already won reelection outright in June with a commanding 63% of the vote). The prospect of a total progressive takeover in the country’s second-largest city would be a major flex for the ascendant DSA — and would make Los Angeles the leading laboratory of progressive governance.
Jeremy B. White: I’ll cheat a bit and say I’m curious to see the fate of three Democratic incumbents facing viable, well-funded Democratic challenges for safe seats: Rep. Doris Matsui in Sacramento, Rep. Mike Thompson in northern California and Rep. Jimmy Gomez in Los Angeles. So much of the focus has deservedly been on whether Democrats win the reconfigured Prop 50 districts to secure a majority. But at a time of generational turnover and roiling anti-establishment discontent — plus a dose of scandal (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/08/19/jimmy-gomez-house-ethics-sexual-misconduct-staffer-01041651), in Gomez’s case — blue seats could flip, too. Democrats will likely reclaim the House. But it’s less clear what they’d do with power — and that’s largely because of the kind of internal divisions on display in these races.
Blake Jones: Moderate Democrat Adam Gray and progressive populist Randy Villegas , who are both running in competitive districts in the Central Valley, could tell us a lot (https://www.politico.com/newsletters/california-playbook/2026/10/09/how-to-win-the-central-valley-01113264) about how the Democratic coalition is moving. Each should perform better than Democrats did in their respective regions in 2024, given the atmosphere we’re in. But if Gray or Villegas does so by a noticeably larger margin, that would be a signal that their brand of politics is faring better in the Valley, and likely, among their districts’ Latino voter majorities. If they perform similarly — or if Gray only gets a slight edge from his incumbency advantage — that would be a sign that voters are simply moving away from Republicans and not toward a specific kind of Democratic message.
Will McCarthy: It has been 15 years since Occupy Wall Street brought the issue of wealth inequality to the center of political discourse in the United States. Billionaires and their bottomless resources had a growing influence over the political system, and the concept of the 1% and the 99% became a familiar part of the American political lexicon.
But years later, through three presidential campaigns and countless Bernie Sanders speeches, voters until now have never had the chance to weigh in on the issue in such a direct way as Proposition 40, a one-time tax on California’s billionaires. The issue pits a fractured coalition against an opponent with endless resources, and the polling suggests the measure is running behind. But will voters, who routinely express a dour view of billionaires (https://www.dataforprogress.org/blog/2026/8/13/voters-think-billionaires-earned-their-wealth-through-exploitation-not-hard-work), vote to pass the measure simply to stick it to the man?
Daniel Miller: Los Angeles’ mayoral race is a strange brew of grievance and policy. Incumbent Karen Bass and Councilmember Nithya Raman , once allies, are now skirmishing over homelessness, housing affordability and how to best prepare for the 2028 Olympics. The race has tightened (https://www.politico.com/newsletters/california-playbook/2026/10/29/karen-bass-is-back-in-the-race-01140222), despite polls showing deep dissatisfaction with the mayor.
Raman, who narrowly bested Spencer Pratt in the primary, has criticized Bass’ homelessness strategy and her plan to loosen short-term-rental rules (https://www.thesportsexaminer.com/los-angeles-2028-l-a-mayor-bass-proposing-rule-change-to-allow-more-airbnb-rentals-in-2028-motions-on-la28-purchases-reimbursements-headed-to-council/) during the Games. Hollywood is another fault line: Raman vows to bring production jobs back, though she recused herself from four of seven council votes (https://www.politico.com/newsletters/california-playbook/2026/10/23/nithya-ramans-answer-to-the-hollywood-question-01133465) on entertainment industry-related measures because her husband works in television. The winner will help lead both the city’s Olympic preparations and its response to Hollywood’s jobs crisis, which has been fomented by years of runaway production (https://www.politico.com/news/magazine/2026/08/16/hollywood-film-production-illinois-tax-credits-01037735?utm_medium=activitypub). A Raman victory would mark a sea change at City Hall and thrust her into the national spotlight, inviting comparisons to New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani — whether or not they hold up (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/02/09/new-mayoral-challenger-in-los-angeles-draws-mamdani-comparisons-00771033) under close examination.
Liam Dillon: Lots of people are talking about the LA mayor’s race and I’ll add to the chorus, but through the lens of housing. A Raman win combined with the expected victory of Janeese Lewis George as mayor of Washington D.C., would be a boon to the burgeoning nationwide “Left-YIMBY (https://x.com/Janeese4DC/status/2109410845113618690)” movement. Raman, Lewis George and Mamdani all are members of the Democratic Socialists of America and promise to expand protections for tenants as part of their agendas. But at the same time, they’ve embraced the role of the private market in housing development and have pledged to remove zoning restrictions and other municipal barriers to growth — policies favored by pro-growth, Yes In My Backyard activists.
As I’ve written, the idea faces healthy skepticism (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/03/07/mamdani-nithya-raman-housing-socialism-abundance-00817314). One centrist critic calls Left-YIMBYism “capitalism for developers, communism for landlords.” But its supporters believe its potential success could end the left’s housing wars and lead to an enduring, renter-centered political coalition.
Tyler Katzenberger: Will tech’s spending spree in state legislative races pay off? A North Bay Assembly contest between fellow Democrats Eric Lucan and Jackie Elward offers a test: Grow California, funded by crypto executives Chris Larsen and Tim Draper , has cumulatively spent more than $1 million backing Lucan and opposing Elward, labor’s favored candidate. A Lucan win would help validate the industry’s strategy of swaying state politics by spending big in Dem-on-Dem races, while an Elward victory would be a triumph for labor leaders who increasingly find themselves at war with tech interests.
The race also has high stakes for Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas , who ruffled feathers among the Legislature’s Black and Progressive caucuses (https://subscriber.politicopro.com/article/2026/11/rivas-assembly-senate-endorsements-01144382) by endorsing Lucan, who is seen as the more moderate candidate, over Elward, a Black woman and self-identified progressive.
Lindsey Holden: Proposition 39, California’s voter ID ballot measure, once looked like it might have a real shot. Polling earlier this year suggested the concept was broadly popular (https://www.politico.com/newsletters/california-playbook-pm/2026/05/04/california-democrats-voter-id-00905425), and Democrats were slow to mount an opposition campaign (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/05/04/californias-fight-against-voter-id-is-a-slow-burn-00905656). But in the months since the primary, voting rights groups, labor, legislative leaders, Gov. Gavin Newsom and his likely successor, Xavier Becerra , all lined up against it (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/07/24/california-dems-ramp-up-anti-voter-id-fight-01011990), relentlessly yoking the measure to Trump.
The messaging seems to have paid off. The measure is trailing in polls (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/10/19/california-voter-id-measure-falling-short-in-new-poll-01127047), and the president’s ongoing efforts to exert control over California’s elections (https://www.politico.com/newsletters/california-playbook-pm/2026/10/15/california-noncitizen-voting-lawsuit-01121542) likely isn’t helping Republican Assemblymember Carl DeMaio create the bipartisan coalition he would have needed to make it law.
Saqib Rahim: The traditionally low-profile race for insurance commissioner has become a dramatic faceoff this year between an up-and-coming progressive, former Sanders campaigner Jane Kim , and an experienced Sacramento Democrat, state Sen. Ben Allen , whose own mom was displaced by the LA fires. On its face, it’s a classic insider-outsider battle. But it’s also become a debate about government: how extensively the government should intervene when people feel crushed by the cost of living, versus trusting market forces to fix things. It’s a debate Republicans and Democrats are having around America about an issue that is only going to become more urgent on a hotter planet.
Alex Nieves: A handful of Assembly races could help progressives gain ground in a chamber dominated by moderates in recent years. That includes the Orange County district where Sanders-backed candidate Jessie Lopez is challenging fellow Democrat David Penaloza . Lopez, a Santa Ana City Council member and member of the Working Families Party, has garnered endorsements from progressives like Assemblymember Alex Lee and state Sen. Caroline Menjivar , while Penaloza has the support of Rivas and the California Democratic Party. The oil industry has also come out against Lopez, contributing to an independent expenditure committee that’s spent more than $1 million to oppose her.

I'm noting that there are no actual results yet, so I'm working from the indicators. The latest independent polls, PPIC and IGS, both show No ahead, with Yes under 50%. SurveyUSA has Yes narrowly ahead at 44–43, and I'm weighing that against the earlier TrueDot/Politico poll.

I'm checking the rest of the poll picture: Politico's undecideds leaning Yes, the AIMSA and Republican-sponsored polls, and the market estimate of roughly one-in-four odds of passage. I'm also weighing the spending gap, the steady slide in Yes support since March, and the historical tendency for measures polling under 50% to fail.

I'm weighing the remaining counterpoints: undecided voters, the possibility that "ballot label" wording skews the polls, and the anti-billionaire sentiment that could push votes toward Yes. Overall I still put Yes around 20–25%, so the answer leans "no," though I want to double-check the IGS poll's methodology and the SurveyUSA and Mason-Dixon details before settling on it.

I'm going to check whether there's a Strength in Numbers or Silver Bulletin polling average for this measure. I also want to see how PPIC and IGS did on California ballot measures in 2024, then read the LA Times write-up of the IGS poll for a breakdown of people who had already voted.

p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text" data-subscriber-content> California voters are souring on a Nov. 3 ballot measure to impose a one-time tax on billionaires to help fund healthcare programs, a proposal that has triggered one of the most expensive political battles in state history.
Half of likely voters plan to vote against Proposition 40, the proposed wealth tax (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-40-billionaire-tax-voter-guide) on billionaires’ assets, while 42% support it, according to a new poll by UC Berkeley’s Institute of Governmental Studies that was co-sponsored by the Los Angeles Times. The findings mark a significant decline in support of the measure, which was crafted by an influential California healthcare union to compensate for an estimated $100 billion in federal healthcare cuts approved by President Trump and congressional Republicans.
The survey also found that a solid majority of likely voters opposed Proposition 39, which would require Californians to provide identification when voting and election officials to verify registered voters are U.S. citizens. The findings come as the Trump administration continues to attack California as a haven for voter fraud, including unfounded allegations of rampant illegal voting by undocumented immigrants.

California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Your guide to Proposition 40: California’s billionaire tax proposal (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-40-billionaire-tax-voter-guide)
Prop 40, which would tax the assets of California billionaires to mostly fund healthcare, has divided Democratic politicians, labor unions and other groups.
Oct. 1, 2026
Mark DiCamillo, the poll’s director, said previous surveys showed support for Proposition 40 has been fragile, and the most recent shows its prospects have dimmed as election day approaches.
The increase in opposition to Proposition 40 is “broad-based and spans virtually all major segments of the electorate,” DiCamillio said. The ballot measure was leading in a Berkeley poll conducted just six weeks ago, albeit by a slim margin, so its reversal of fortune is significant, he said.
Advertisement
The declining support comes after an onslaught of money spent opposing Proposition 40, including a torrent of television and social media ads airing everywhere from NFL games to “Everybody Loves Raymond” reruns. Nearly $368 million has been contributed to efforts opposing the billionaire tax, while $36 million has been donated to support the proposed levy.
Proposition 40 would impose a one-time 5% tax on the assets of billionaires who resided in California as of Jan. 1, with some exceptions. Democrats and their allies are splintered over the proposal. Some, including Gov. Gavin Newsom, argue it will prompt the wealthy to flee California, further harming its volatile budget, which is dependent on the state’s richest residents. The California Democratic Party and leading progressives support the measure, with Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) calling it a modest tax necessary to help Californians struggling because of cuts imposed by Republicans to pay for tax breaks for the wealthy.
While Republican voters overwhelmingly oppose Proposition 40, nearly two-thirds of Democrats support it and more than a quarter opposing it. There is also a generational divide, with 6 out of 10 voters 65 years old or older opposing the measure, while more than two-thirds of those under 30 supporting it, according to the poll.
The findings are similar to a Public Policy Institute of California poll released Tuesday, which found 52% of likely voters would vote against Proposition 40, while 46% supported it.
The campaign against the wealth tax, funded by some of California’s richest tech moguls, is centered on three intertwined ballot initiatives: Proposition 40 and Propositions 41 and 42, both of which would undercut Proposition 40 through a series of changes to state tax laws and spending restrictions.
Proposition 41 would cut wasteful government spending (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-41-tax-audit-voter-guide) by requiring audits of new state special taxes and would bar new state taxes that are exempt from a state spending limit. Proposition 42 would prohibit new taxes on retirement holdings, individually owned assets and other personal savings. Both Propositions 41 and 42 would nullify the billionaire tax if it passes, provided either measure receives more votes.
A plurality of voters oppose Propositions 41 and 42, a reversal from just six week ago, according to the poll.
In mid-September, voters were closely divided about Proposition 41 — 37% in favor and 33% opposed — (https://escholarship.org/uc/item/2zw023kt) with a large number of undecided. In the current poll, 38% of likely voters favor the measure and 47% oppose it. Proposition 42 led by 9 percentage points in the Berkeley/L.A. Times poll in September — 43% in favor and 34% opposed. Now, 43% of likely voters support it and 45% oppose it.
DiCamillo said backers of a ballot measure also should be concerned any time support registers below 50%, since voters who are undecided or unsure tend to vote no.
“It’s below 50%, and it’s trending down. Both of those are ominous signs,” DiCamillo said. Proposition 42 is “still very close. I’m not saying it’s definitely going down, but it’s moving in the wrong direction late in the campaign, and usually movement in a late poll is even more significant than the actual numbers themselves.”
He added that while many voters were unaware the two proposed ballot measures were designed as poison pills to kill the billionaire tax, among those who knew, the opposition was significantly greater.

Where does California’s Prop 40 stand? Here’s what the latest polls say
As voters get ready to cast their ballots this week, polls show that Prop 40 is losing support
By Danielle Echeverria (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/danielle-echeverria/) , Staff Writer Nov 2, 2026
Attendees in San Francisco cheer during a “Ballots Over Billionaires” wealth tax rally on San Francisco, Saturday, Oct. 3, 2026. Polls show support for the proposed tax in decline.
Stephen Lam/S.F. Chronicle
Recent polls show that the so-called billionaire tax is losing steam among California voters.
Arguably the two most reputable pollsters of California are UC Berkeley’s Institute of Governmental Studies and the Public Policy Institute of California. Both found last month that support for Proposition 40 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/election/article/prop-40-41-42-california-22476000.php), which would impose a one-time, 5% wealth tax on California residents worth more than $1 billion, has declined, leaving neither side with a clear lead.
Election guide: What you need to know to vote on California's 2026 propositions (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/california-ballot-measures-propositions-22507044.php)
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
The results are a departure from earlier surveys by the same pollsters, which both found the “Yes” side leading the “No” in their September polls.
Loading...
The October poll from the Public Policy Institute of California (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/), a nonpartisan think tank, found that 46% of likely voters said they would vote yes on the proposed tax, down from 52% in September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/): The numbers in opposition moved in mirror image, with the share opposing the measure growing from 46% to 52%.
Election Endorsements: Will the billionaire tax Prop 40 actually help California? (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-40-tax-billionaire-california-22477038.php)
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Polling from Berkeley IGS found a similar trend. In October (https://escholarship.org/uc/item/72722408), IGS found 50% of likely voters intended to vote no on the tax, while 42% planned to vote yes, with 8% undecided. A month earlier, just 42% planned to vote no on the tax, while 45% planned to vote yes.
Not every poll found that support for the tax is lagging. In early October, a Politico poll (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/10/19/california-billionaire-tax-poll-01125462) found that 46% of likely voters planned to vote Yes on Prop. 40, while 43% planned to vote no, with the rest undecided, essentially the same finding as it had a month earlier. But that level of support would still not be enough support to get the tax over the finish line. And as pollsters have argued (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/4-high-profile-ballot-measures-leading-in-state-9237930.php?utm_source=chatgpt.com), tax measures that cannot poll above 50% generally fail, even if they seem ahead.
Loading...
The proposition needs more than 50% of the vote to pass, though that also depends on the fate of two other ballot measures: The one time tax will take effect only if Props 41 and 42 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/election/article/prop-40-41-42-california-22476000.php), which have provisions that conflict with Prop 40, fail. The two competing propositions were created and submitted by Building a Better California (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/billionaire-tax-california-pac-22442333.php), the political action committee set up by billionaires opposing Prop 40.
Opponents of the proposed tax have raised hundreds of millions of dollars to defeat it, and most of that funding has come from the billionaires themselves. The opponents argue that the tax will drive the state’s wealthiest residents away, decreasing tax revenue in the long run (https://www.sfchronicle.com/california/article/billionaire-tax-analysis-22485993.php). Prominent Democrats have also come out in opposition to the tax, including Governor Gavin Newsom (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/gavin-newsom-ballot-propositions-22470170.php), gubernatorial candidate Xavier Becerra and former Congresswoman Katie Porter (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/openforum/article/prop-40-billionaires-tax-katie-porter-california-22433287.php).
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
But the tax still has support among progressives like Bernie Sanders (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/openforum/article/billionaire-tax-california-prop-40-22458432.php), Rep. Ro Khanna (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/joegarofoli/article/prop-40-tom-steyer-22455442.php) and billionaire climate activist Tom Steyer. Supporters argue that the tax, which is intended to backfill federal cuts to the state’s healthcare funding, will keep people from losing their Medi-Cal benefits.
